title: Black Sea Cuisine Guide: Mıhlama, Hamsi, Pide & Cornbread
seoTitle: Black Sea Cuisine Guide: Mıhlama, Hamsi, Pide & Cornbread

quickAnswer: Northern Türkiye's kitchen runs on alpine butter, coarse stone-ground cornmeal, winter anchovies (hamsi), dark collard greens, and wood-fired flatbreads. From stretchy Trabzon kuymak and mıhlama at breakfast to closed Bafra pide, open-faced Sürmene cheese boats, and pepper-dusted sweet Laz böreği, Black Sea cooking is hearty, rain-fed, and deeply seasonal.

body.text: Planning a trip around black sea food turkey introduces flavours far removed from Mediterranean olive oil. Steep, misty mountains trap rainfall along the coast from Samsun to Artvin—a coastline highlighted in [GoTürkiye's announcement of National Geographic's Best of the World 2026](https://goturkiye.com/branding/press-releases/turkiyes-black-sea-coast-chosen-in-national-geographics)—producing lush highland pastures, world-leading hazelnuts, and dense golden cornmeal (mısır unu) that anchors regional bread and fish dishes.
What is the difference between mıhlama (kuymak) made with Trabzon butter and kolot cheese?

Mıhlama (commonly called kuymak in Trabzon) is a hot copper-pan fondue of slow-toasted cornmeal, alpine butter, and stretchy mountain cheese. While cooks use both names interchangeably across the coast, local purists distinguish them by ratio: Trabzon kuymak leans slightly heavier on roasted cornmeal and buttery richness, whereas Rize mıhlama emphasises maximum elastic cheese pull.

The secret lies in two non-negotiable ingredients: Trabzon butter (Trabzon tereyağı) churned from high-altitude pasture cream, and aged kolot or telli (çeçil) cheese that melts into long ribbons without turning greasy. As [GoTürkiye's Taste the Flavors of Black Sea Region guide](https://goturkiye.com/blacksea/taste) notes, authentic kuymak is cooked slowly until golden butter pools cleanly at the surface. Always tear off warm mısır ekmeği (dense, unsweetened Black Sea cornbread) or crusty Vakfıkebir sourdough to scoop it straight from the copper pan before it cools and sets.

body.text: When is fresh hamsi (Black Sea anchovy) season (November–February)?

Fresh hamsi season runs from late autumn through mid-winter, peaking between November and February after cold northern winds drop Black Sea water temperatures. Only when the water chills does the small migratory anchovy build the subcutaneous fat layer that makes pan-fried hamsi tava and baked hamsili pilav rich and tender.

According to [GoTürkiye's Black Sea culinary guide](https://goturkiye.com/blacksea/taste), coastal cooks serve anchovies dozens of ways—layered into spiced rice with currants (hamsili pilav), baked inside herbed cornbread (hamsi ekmeği), or dusted in cornmeal and pan-fried in a neat wheel (hamsi tava). Outside November through February, restaurants often serve frozen fillets; confirm the fish arrived fresh that morning before ordering.
Why is Bafra and Sürmene pide famous across Türkiye?

Black Sea pide stands apart for hand-stretched, paper-thin dough baked in roaring wood-fired stone ovens and generously brushed with cultured highland butter the moment it leaves the hearth. Bafra pidesi from Samsun is long, narrow, and sealed shut around savoury minced meat, whereas Sürmene pidesi from Trabzon stays open-faced and overflowing with molten mountain cheese.

Both styles carry formal Geographical Indication protection. As documented by the [Bafra Municipality](https://www.bafra.bel.tr/Sayfa/5fc09f8dfdcac104104ae3d2/BAFRA-PIDESI-VE-NOKULU), Bafra Pidesi was registered by the Turkish Patent and Trademark Office on 18 November 2009: it stretches 70 to 75 centimetres long, stays crisp on the edges, and is sliced into six pieces right after buttering. Further east, Sürmene Pidesi ([KÜRE Encyclopedia — Sürmene Pide](https://kureansiklopedi.com/en/detay/surmene-pide-3cdf7)) is traditionally baked with local melting cheese—and optionally topped with a fresh farm egg cracked into the centre just before finishing—so diners tear off the crisp rim and dip it into the centre.
What is Laz böreği and why is it sweet?

Despite sharing a name with savoury Turkish börek pastries, Laz böreği is a warm, syrup-soaked custard dessert originating from the Laz communities of eastern Artvin and Rize. Paper-thin phyllo sheets encase a silky vanilla-and-egg milk pudding, finished with light sugar syrup and a surprising pinch of freshly cracked black pepper.

[GoTürkiye's Taste the Flavors of Artvin guide](https://goturkiye.com/artvin/taste) notes that Hopa Laz Böreği holds Geographical Indication status, specifying the signature black pepper sprinkled right before baking finishes to cut the custard's sweetness. Before you head north—or link a coastal itinerary with historic Marmara stops such as our [Bursa destination guide](https://itineraryofturkiye.com/destinations/bursa)—keep this Black Sea tasting checklist handy:

items: Pair heavy dairy with Rize tea: Roughly 60 percent of Türkiye's tea grows in Rize; a tulip glass of brisk black tea cuts right through butter-rich pide and mıhlama.
Order karalahana çorbası: Do not overlook dark collard-green soup cooked with red kidney beans and cracked corn—it is the daily comfort dish of village homes.
Ask for fresh hamsi dates: Order hamsi tava primarily from November through February; choose Black Sea trout (alabalık) cooked in butter during warmer summer months.
Eat pide immediately: Both Bafra and Sürmene crusts soften within ten minutes of cooling, so dine in rather than ordering takeaway.

faq.q: Can vegetarians eat well in the Black Sea region?
faq.a: Yes. Beyond butter-rich mıhlama, cheese Sürmene pide, and cornbread, regional kitchens serve braised collard greens (karalahana), pickled green beans (fasulye turşusu kavurması), and wild mountain greens sautéed with onion.

faq.q: Is Black Sea cornbread sweet like American cornbread?
faq.a: No. Traditional mısır ekmeği is savoury, dense, and crumbly, made with stone-ground yellow or white cornmeal, water, salt, and little to no sugar so it pairs naturally with yoghurt, fish, and soups.

faq.q: Why do Trabzon locals crack an egg on top of Sürmene pide?
faq.a: Cracking a raw egg into the hot cheese filling during the final minute of baking creates a glossy, custardy centre that diners stir into the molten cheese with torn pieces of crust.

faq.q: Where can you try authentic Black Sea food in Istanbul?
faq.a: Several long-running Trabzon and Rize kitchens operate in Kadıköy, Beşiktaş, and Üsküdar, shipping in highland butter, kolot cheese, and stone-ground cornmeal weekly from the coast.
Hamsiköy sütlaç is a slow-simmered, oven-browned rice pudding named after a mountain village near Trabzon, prized for rich alpine pasture milk and served topped with crushed Giresun hazelnuts.

faq.q: How does Black Sea butter differ from supermarket butter?
faq.a: Highland pastures around Trabzon and Rize contain diverse wildflowers and herbs, giving small-batch churned butter a deep yellow colour and distinct grassy aroma essential to authentic kuymak.
